name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q01 - Steps in the process of decomposition

questiontext.text:
Match the steps of decomposition with their correct descriptions:

StepDescription
A. Fragmentation(i) Accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance resistant to microbial action
B. Leaching(ii) Breakdown of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores
C. Catabolism(iii) Degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances by bacterial and fungal enzymes
D. Humification(iv) Water-soluble inorganic nutrients going down into the soil horizon and precipitating as unavailable salts

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Decomposition involves five simultaneous processes acting on detritus: fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, and mineralisation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Process
- Fragmentation is the mechanical breakdown of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores such as earthworms.
- Leaching is the process by which water-soluble inorganic nutrients percolate down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
- Catabolism is the enzymatic degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances by bacterial and fungal enzymes.
- Humification leads to the accumulation of humus, a dark-coloured, colloidal, amorphous substance that is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes extremely slowly.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Fragmentation matches breakdown of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores; Leaching matches water-soluble inorganic nutrients going down into the soil horizon and precipitating as unavailable salts; Catabolism matches degradation of detritus into simpler inorganic substances by bacterial and fungal enzymes; Humification matches accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance resistant to microbial action (A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(iii), D-(i)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q02 - Trophic levels and representative organisms

questiontext.text:
Match each trophic level with its representative examples in an ecosystem:

Trophic LevelExamples
A. First trophic level(i) Birds, fishes, wolf
B. Second trophic level(ii) Phytoplankton, grass, trees
C. Third trophic level(iii) Man, lion
D. Fourth trophic level(iv) Zooplankton, grasshopper, cow

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Organisms occupy a specific trophic level in a food chain based on their source of nutrition or food.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Trophic Level
- The first trophic level consists of autotrophic producers (plants), such as phytoplankton, grass, and trees.
- The second trophic level consists of primary consumers (herbivores), such as zooplankton, grasshoppers, and cows.
- The third trophic level consists of secondary consumers (primary carnivores), such as birds, fishes, and wolves.
- The fourth trophic level consists of tertiary consumers (top carnivores), such as man and lion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: First trophic level matches phytoplankton, grass, trees; Second trophic level matches zooplankton, grasshopper, cow; Third trophic level matches birds, fishes, wolf; Fourth trophic level matches man, lion (A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q03 - Primary production and productivity definitions

questiontext.text:
Match the productivity terms with their correct definitions and units:

TermDefinition / Unit
A. Primary production(i) Available biomass for consumption by heterotrophs
B. Productivity(ii) Amount of biomass produced per unit area over a time period, expressed in \(\text{g m}^{-2}\)
C. Gross primary productivity(iii) Rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis
D. Net primary productivity(iv) Rate of biomass production, expressed in \(\text{g m}^{-2}\text{ yr}^{-1}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ecosystem energy capture by autotrophs is quantified using distinct terms for total biomass accumulated, rate of production, and biomass remaining after plant respiration.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
- Primary production is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis, expressed in weight (\(\text{g m}^{-2}\)) or energy (\(\text{kcal m}^{-2}\)).
- Productivity is the rate of biomass production, expressed in \(\text{g m}^{-2}\text{ yr}^{-1}\) or \((\text{kcal m}^{-2})\text{ yr}^{-1}\) to compare different ecosystems.
- Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis.
- Net primary productivity (NPP) is \(\text{GPP} - R\) (respiration losses), which represents the available biomass for consumption by heterotrophs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Primary production matches amount of biomass produced per unit area over a time period in \(\text{g m}^{-2}\); Productivity matches rate of biomass production in \(\text{g m}^{-2}\text{ yr}^{-1}\); Gross primary productivity matches rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis; Net primary productivity matches available biomass for consumption by heterotrophs (A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(iii), D-(i)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q04 - Key terms in ecological succession

questiontext.text:
Match the ecological succession terms with their correct meanings:

TermMeaning
A. Pioneer species(i) Entire sequence of communities that successively change in a given area
B. Climax community(ii) Community that is in near equilibrium with the environment
C. Sere(iii) Succession taking place in wet areas progressing from hydric to mesic conditions
D. Hydrarch succession(iv) Species that invade a bare area

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ecological succession is the orderly, sequential, and fairly predictable change in the species composition of a given area over time.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
- Pioneer species are the organisms (such as lichens on bare rock or small phytoplanktons in water) that first invade a bare area.
- The climax community is the final stable community that reaches near equilibrium with the environment.
- A sere is the entire sequence of communities that successively change in a given area, with individual transitional communities termed seral stages.
- Hydrarch succession takes place in wet areas and progresses from hydric to mesic conditions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Pioneer species matches species that invade a bare area; Climax community matches community in near equilibrium with the environment; Sere matches entire sequence of communities successively changing in an area; Hydrarch succession matches succession in wet areas progressing from hydric to mesic conditions (A-(iv), B-(ii), C-(i), D-(iii)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q05 - Seral stages of primary succession in water

questiontext.text:
Match the stages of primary succession in water with their corresponding plant communities:

StageCommunity
A. Pioneer stage(i) Forest
B. Second stage(ii) Small phytoplanktons
C. Stage preceding marsh-meadow(iii) Reed-swamp stage
D. Climax stage(iv) Rooted-submerged plants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In primary succession in water (hydrarch succession), the aquatic habitat is gradually converted into a mesic land community through an orderly sequence of seral stages.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Stage
The sequential order of communities in primary succession in water is: small phytoplanktons (pioneer stage) \(\rightarrow\) rooted-submerged plants (second stage) \(\rightarrow\) rooted-floating angiosperms and free-floating plants \(\rightarrow\) reed-swamp stage (immediately preceding marsh-meadow) \(\rightarrow\) marsh-meadow stage \(\rightarrow\) scrub stage \(\rightarrow\) forest (climax stage).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Pioneer stage matches small phytoplanktons; Second stage matches rooted-submerged plants; Stage preceding marsh-meadow matches reed-swamp stage; Climax stage matches forest (A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(iii), D-(i)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q06 - Nutrient cycling and standing quantities

questiontext.text:
Match the ecological concepts with their accurate descriptions:

ConceptDescription
A. Standing state(i) Mass of living material at a trophic level at a particular time
B. Standing crop(ii) Amount of nutrients present in the soil at any given time
C. Gaseous nutrient cycle(iii) Phosphorus and sulphur cycles with reservoir in Earth's crust
D. Sedimentary nutrient cycle(iv) Nitrogen and carbon cycles with reservoir in the atmosphere

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ecosystems maintain both living biomass pools and abiotic nutrient reservoirs, and biogeochemical cycles are classified based on the location of their main reservoir.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Standing state refers to the amount of nutrients (such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium) present in the soil at any given time.
- Standing crop refers to the mass of living material (biomass) or number of organisms at each trophic level at a particular time.
- Gaseous nutrient cycles (e.g., nitrogen and carbon cycles) have their reservoir in the atmosphere.
- Sedimentary nutrient cycles (e.g., phosphorus and sulphur cycles) have their reservoir located in the Earth's crust.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Standing state matches amount of nutrients present in the soil at any given time; Standing crop matches mass of living material at a trophic level at a particular time; Gaseous nutrient cycle matches nitrogen and carbon cycles with reservoir in the atmosphere; Sedimentary nutrient cycle matches phosphorus and sulphur cycles with reservoir in Earth's crust (A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(iii)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q07 - Quantitative ecosystem values and percentages

questiontext.text:
Match the ecosystem parameters with their respective quantitative values:

Ecosystem ParameterQuantitative Value
A. Annual NPP of the oceans(i) \(2\text{--}10\%\)
B. Percentage of global carbon dissolved in oceans(ii) About \(50\%\)
C. Percentage of PAR captured by plants(iii) \(55\text{ billion tons}\)
D. Share of soil formation in total ecosystem services cost(iv) \(71\%\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Global ecological fluxes and valuations—spanning ocean productivity, carbon reservoirs, solar energy capture, and ecosystem services—are quantified with specific benchmark values.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Parameter
- Out of the \(170\text{ billion tons}\) of annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere, the productivity of the oceans is only \(55\text{ billion tons}\).
- Of the total quantity of global carbon, \(71\%\) is found dissolved in oceans, which regulates atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\).
- Plants capture only \(2\text{--}10\%\) of the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), and this small amount sustains the entire living world.
- Out of the total estimated cost of various ecosystem services (US \(\$33\text{ trillion}\) a year), soil formation accounts for about \(50\%\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Annual NPP of the oceans matches \(55\text{ billion tons}\); Percentage of global carbon dissolved in oceans matches \(71\%\); Percentage of PAR captured by plants matches \(2\text{--}10\%\); Share of soil formation in total ecosystem services cost matches about \(50\%\) (A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ECOSYSTEM_MATCH_Q08 - Pond ecosystem structural and functional components

questiontext.text:
Match the components of a pond ecosystem with their representative constituents:

Pond Ecosystem ComponentRepresentative Constituents
A. Abiotic component(i) Zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms
B. Autotrophic component(ii) Fungi, bacteria and flagellates abundant at the bottom
C. Consumer component(iii) Water with dissolved substances and rich soil deposit at the bottom
D. Decomposer component(iv) Phytoplankton, algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A pond is a self-sustainable shallow aquatic ecosystem that exhibits all four basic functional components through its abiotic and biotic constituents.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Component
- The abiotic component of a pond is the water with all dissolved inorganic and organic substances and the rich soil deposit at the bottom.
- The autotrophic component includes phytoplankton, some algae, and the floating, submerged, and marginal plants found at the edges.
- The consumers are represented by zooplankton, free-swimming forms, and bottom-dwelling forms.
- The decomposers are fungi, bacteria, and flagellates, which are especially abundant at the bottom of the pond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: Abiotic component matches water with dissolved substances and rich soil deposit at the bottom; Autotrophic component matches phytoplankton, algae, floating, submerged and marginal plants; Consumer component matches zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms; Decomposer component matches fungi, bacteria and flagellates abundant at the bottom (A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii)).
